zebralogic.title: Consolidate Direct Equivalences
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly equates two or more attribute values (e.g., "Alice is the person who loves rock music"), merge them into a single composite fact and propagate that fact to all related attributes.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Immediately after parsing any clue that states equality between attributes.
zebralogic.example: Treating "Alice is the person who loves rock music" as two separate facts and assigning rock music to a different house, breaking the equivalence.

zebralogic.title: Assign Fixed Positions Immediately
zebralogic.principle: If a clue pins an attribute to a specific house number (e.g., "The person with fish is in the fourth house"), place that attribute (and any directly linked attributes) in that house right away.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: As soon as a fixed‑position clue is identified.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring "The person who uses a Samsung Galaxy S21 is in the second house" and later putting that phone model in a different house.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Adjacency for 'next to' and Ordered Left
zebralogic.principle: Adjacency clues ('next to', 'directly left of', 'directly right of') require the two referenced houses to differ by exactly one position, with the correct left/right orientation.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When processing any adjacency or direct‑left/right clue.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "A is directly left of B" as "A can be anywhere left of B", resulting in non‑adjacent placements.

zebralogic.title: Output Solution in Expected JSON Table Format
zebralogic.principle: The verifier expects a JSON object with a "header" array listing column names and a "rows" array of string arrays; any deviation (missing header, extra fields, wrong ordering) causes rejection.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After solving, before emitting the final answer.
zebralogic.example: Returning a plain‑text table or omitting the "header" key, which prevents the parser from extracting the solution.

zebralogic.title: Keep Reasoning Concise to Avoid Token Truncation
zebralogic.principle: The model has a limited token budget; overly long reasoning can truncate the final JSON, making the answer invalid. Summarise reasoning and place the JSON at the very end.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Throughout the solution process; ensure the final output fits within the token limit.
zebralogic.example: Writing a lengthy step‑by‑step narrative that cuts off the JSON before the last row, resulting in a missing cell.

zebralogic.title: Preserve Original Attribute Tokens (Case and Spelling)
zebralogic.principle: Attribute values must be reproduced exactly as given (including case, spaces, punctuation); any alteration leads to a mismatch with the reference solution.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When writing the final JSON rows.
zebralogic.example: Writing "rock" instead of "Rock" or adding an extra space, causing the verifier to reject the answer.

zebralogic.title: Directional Ordering for 'somewhere to the left/right of' constraints
zebralogic.principle: Clues that say "X is somewhere to the left/right of Y" impose a strict ordering: house(X) < house(Y) for left, house(X) > house(Y) for right. No adjacency is required.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing any non‑adjacent ordering clue.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "A is somewhere to the right of B" as A left of B, producing reversed positions.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Exclusion Constraints for Specific House Numbers
zebralogic.principle: If a clue forbids an attribute from a particular house (e.g., "The Huawei phone is not in the fifth house"), remove that house from the attribute's possible domain immediately.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: As soon as an exclusion clue is read.
zebralogic.example: Allowing the Huawei phone to be placed in house 5 despite the clue, later causing a conflict.

zebralogic.title: Transitive Ordering Inference
zebralogic.principle: When multiple direct ordering clues form a chain (e.g., A left of B and B left of C), infer the implied indirect ordering (A left of C) to further prune positions.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After collecting all ordering clues, before final assignment.
zebralogic.example: Failing to deduce that A must be left of C, leaving an impossible configuration that later violates another clue.

zebralogic.title: Interpret Directional Ordering Correctly
zebralogic.principle: For any clue containing "somewhere to the right of" or "somewhere to the left of", enforce the inequality in the correct direction: the first entity must be placed strictly to the right (higher house number) or left (lower house number) of the second entity. Verify the inequality after placement to avoid swapping the entities.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a directional ordering clue is processed.
zebralogic.example: Misreading "The mother of Timothy is somewhere to the right of the cruise lover" and placing the mother left of the cruise lover, violating the clue.

zebralogic.description: Generating overly long reasoning before the final answer, causing token truncation.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model tries to be thorough and includes many intermediate steps, exceeding the token budget.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Keep reasoning concise, place the JSON at the very end, and monitor token usage.

zebralogic.description: Providing the solution in a format not recognized by the verifier.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model is unaware of the exact JSON schema expected by the verifier.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Follow the exact format: a JSON object with a "header" array and a "rows" array of string arrays.

zebralogic.description: Using incorrect case or synonyms for attribute values.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalises text or substitutes similar words, altering the required tokens.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute tokens verbatim from the puzzle statement, preserving case, spaces, and punctuation.

zebralogic.description: Misinterpreting adjacency constraints that involve a named entity and a non‑name attribute, treating them as non‑adjacent or placing both in the same house.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: Confusion between entity types leads the model to think adjacency only applies within the same attribute category.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Treat adjacency as a positional relation between houses, regardless of which attribute the entities belong to.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: Ambiguity in natural‑language parsing causes the model to swap the subject and reference or invert the inequality.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Explicitly map "right of" → higher house index and "left of" → lower house index, then double‑check the inequality after placement.
